Infeasible means not able to be done or carried out in practice. When something is infeasible, it cannot be successfully achieved given real-world conditions — the barriers standing in the way (like cost, time, resources, technology, or logic) are simply too great to overcome.
The Key Idea Behind the Word

Think of any plan, idea, or task. For it to work, certain conditions need to be met — you need enough money, enough time, the right tools, the right people, and so on. When those conditions cannot realistically be met, the plan is infeasible — it just won't work in the real world.

"Building a hospital in three days is infeasible — there isn't enough time or workforce to make it happen."

The word is a judgment: someone has looked at what a task requires and concluded that it simply cannot be done the way things currently stand.
Infeasible vs. Impossible — A Critical Distinction

This is the most important nuance to understand about this word, and most learners miss it.

Impossible means something cannot happen at all — it defies the laws of nature, logic, or reality itself.

  • "It is impossible to travel back in time."

Infeasible means something could theoretically happen but cannot be done in practice given real constraints like money, time, technology, or effort.

  • "Sending a human to Mars next week is infeasible." (Not impossible — humans have gone to space — but the time, preparation, and resources needed make it unworkable right now.)

In short: impossible closes the door permanently. Infeasible means the door exists, but you currently can't get through it.
What Makes Something Infeasible?

Infeasibility always has a reason — a real, practical barrier. Here are the most common causes:

1. Not enough money

"The proposed stadium renovation is financially infeasible — it would cost ten times the city's annual budget."

2. Not enough time

"Completing 500 pages of legal documents by tomorrow morning is infeasible."

3. Lacking the right technology

"In the 1950s, sending a message instantly across the world was considered infeasible."

4. Not enough people or resources

"With a team of two, finishing this construction project in a month is infeasible."

5. Logical or structural barriers

"The plan requires two things to happen simultaneously in different cities — that's infeasible with only one team."
How and Where the Word is Used

"Infeasible" is a formal word. You will mostly see it in:

  • Business and planning: "The board declared the merger infeasible after reviewing the financials."
  • Engineering and science: "The design was deemed infeasible due to material limitations."
  • Law and policy: "The proposed regulation was found to be infeasible to enforce."
  • Everyday formal speech: "Working two full-time jobs while studying is infeasible for most people."

In casual conversation, people tend to say "not doable," "not realistic," or "can't be done" instead — but in professional or academic settings, infeasible is the precise and preferred term.
Common Patterns You'll See

The word almost always appears in these structures:

  • "It is infeasible to [do something]" → "It is infeasible to redesign the entire system in one week."
  • "[Something] is infeasible" → "The plan is infeasible."
  • "[Something] is infeasible given [condition]" → "The project is infeasible given our current budget."
  • "deemed / considered / found infeasible" → "The proposal was deemed infeasible by the committee."

You'll also see it modified to pinpoint what kind of infeasibility:

  • Technically infeasible — the technology doesn't exist or doesn't work well enough.
  • Financially infeasible — it costs more than what's available or reasonable.
  • Logistically infeasible — the coordination, movement, or organization required simply can't happen.
  • Practically infeasible — a broader term meaning it just won't work in the real world, even if no single specific reason dominates.
The Opposite: Feasible

The opposite of infeasible is feasible, which means able to be done; workable; realistic. Understanding both words together makes each one sharper:

Feasible"We have the budget, time, and team — this is feasible."
Infeasible"We don't have the budget or the time — this is infeasible."

When someone conducts a "feasibility study," they are asking: Is this plan feasible, or is it infeasible? They examine the real-world conditions to decide whether the goal can actually be achieved.
Words Close in Meaning — and How They Differ

These words are related to "infeasible" but are not identical:

  • Impossible — Stronger. Cannot happen at all, ever. (Infeasible just means not workable right now or under current conditions.)
  • Impractical — Weaker. It can be done, but it's inconvenient, inefficient, or unwise. (Infeasible means it genuinely cannot be done, not just that it's a bad idea.)
  • Unworkable — Very close in meaning. Usually used for plans or systems that won't function as intended. (Slightly more informal than infeasible.)
  • Unrealistic — Close, but more about expectations being out of touch with reality. (Infeasible is more objective and grounded in specific, concrete barriers.)
  • Unachievable — Means the goal cannot be reached. (Similar to infeasible but slightly more about the end result than the process.)
A Few More Examples to Cement It

• "The teacher asked for a 10,000-word essay due in one hour. That's infeasible."
  • "It is infeasible to heat an entire city using a single small generator."
  • "Their business model was infeasible — they were spending three dollars for every dollar they earned."
  • "Scientists once thought flying was infeasible, until the Wright Brothers proved otherwise." (This last example beautifully shows that infeasibility is often temporary — tied to current conditions, not eternal truth.)
The One-Sentence Summary

Infeasible means something cannot be done in practice because the real-world barriers — whether of money, time, technology, resources, or logic — are too great to overcome, even if the idea itself isn't outright impossible.
